newsitem.title: TANZANIA: U.N. Rwanda crimes suspect examines torture victim.
newsitem.headline: U.N. Rwanda crimes suspect examines torture victim.

text.p: A Hutu former mayor standing trial for genocide at the U.N.'s criminal tribunal for Rwanda on Wednesday cross-examined a coffee farmer who claims he was beaten and tortured by the accused.
Jean-Paul Akayesu, 43, the former mayor of Rwanda's central Taba commune, cross-examined witness "C", a Hutu farmer code-named to protect his identity.

Akayesu is accused of genocide and crimes against humanity during the mass killings of an estimated 800,000 Tutsis and moderate Hutus in 1994 sparked off by the assassination of Hutu president and military strongman, Juvenal Habyarimana.
Angry Habyarimana supporters took up arms and hunted down Tutsis and moderate Hutus opposed to his junta.
The encounter brought accused and alleged victim face-to- face forcing the witness to relive his ordeal in detail.
"I was bleeding because Akayesu stepped on my face with his shoe. I tried to get up and I had a bloody nose and wounds on my back," the witness said, responding to a question from Akayesu.

The witness stripped off his shirt for a second time on Wednesday to show the court scars received when he said he was tortured and beaten by Akayesu and Hutu interahamwe militiamen one night during the 1994 genocide.

Akayesu took the witness into a forest with Interahamwe militia, made him to lie on his back and then beat him with gun butts with Akayesu stamping on his face before tying him by the neck so that he vomited.
Witness C said he still suffered headaches and nose-bleeds from the incident but was too poor to go to a doctor.
"Why did Akayesu not kill you," Akayesu asked about events the next morning.
"He knows himself because he fetched me and then afterwards he told me to go home," the witness replied.

Akayesu's questions and those later put by defence counsellors Patrice Monthe of Senegal and Nicolas Tiangaye of the Central African Republic clarified details of the witness's testimony but did not dispute the essence of his story.

Akayesu is the first suspect to be tried before the International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda set up to bring to justice the architects of the 1994 Rwandan genocide, which was only by Tutsi rebels now in power.
He has pleaded not guilty to charges of genocide and crimes against humanity. If convicted he will face life imprisonment, the tribunal's highest penalty.
Under court rules the accused has the right to put questions directly.
Akayesu confined since last May to U.N. remand cells near the court was much happier now he had a leading role to play in his own trial, sources at the court told Reuters.
Presiding Judge Laity Kama will rule later this week on Akayesu's earlier request to fire his lawyers assigned to him after he twice dismissed previous counsel.
Akayesu, wearing a dark suit with a sheaf of papers on his knee, asked questions from behind a screen flanked by two security guards.
Earlier witness K, a Rwandan Tutsi accountant in Akayesu's office said she witnessed Akayesu order eight Tutsis hacked to death on April 19, 1994.
In all 21 people have been indicted by the tribunal of whom seven are in custody at tribunal headquarters in Arusha.
Separate trials have also started in the Rwandan capital Kigali and in other towns of the tiny tea and coffee-growing central African nation.
Rwanda holds about 90,000 people suspected of taking part in the genocide but has only just started putting them on trial. Two Hutu men were sentenced to death in Kibungo on January 3.
